title: Old-Time Manure Hotbed
subtitle: How Farmers Got Early Plants
items: Dig a pit in a sunny, dry spot
Let it heat, turn it once
Top with 4-6 in. of good soil
Vent the glass on sunny days
intro: Before electric heat mats, USDA Farmers' Bulletins taught gardeners to warm a seedbed with fermenting manure under a glass sash. The rotting manure gives off steady heat for weeks, so cabbage, lettuce and tomato plants get a head start while snow is still on the ground. Here is the old method in our own words.
desc: Old-time manure hotbed from the USDA Farmers' Bulletins: pack fresh horse manure and straw into a pit, cover it with soil and a glass sash, and let the natural heat start early cabbage, lettuce and tomato seedlings in late winter. Old-fashioned wisdom for self-sufficient gardeners. Full list on the blog.

title: How to Can Apple Butter
subtitle: USDA-Tested Water Bath Method
items: Cook soft in cider and vinegar
intro: Apple butter is one of the easiest preserves for a beginner, and it uses up a pile of apples. These steps follow the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning: cook it down until a spoonful holds its shape with no liquid around the edge, then process in a boiling water bath.
desc: How to can apple butter the USDA-tested way: cook tart apples soft in cider and vinegar, puree, add sugar and spices, simmer until thick, fill hot jars with 1/4-inch headspace and process half-pints or pints 5 minutes in a boiling water bath, adjusting for altitude. Full list on the blog.

title: Pressure Canner Care Checklist
subtitle: Keep It Safe Year After Year
items: Test a dial gauge every year
desc: Pressure canner care checklist for beginners: have a dial gauge tested for accuracy every year, replace hard or cracked gaskets, keep the vent pipe clear and store the canner dry with the lid upside down so it is safe and ready next season. See the canning gear you need. (Contains affiliate links.)

title: Overwinter Spinach for Spring
subtitle: The Earliest Greens You'll Pick
items: Cover with row cover or straw
Uncover as days warm in spring
intro: Spinach is one of the hardiest garden greens. Small plants that get established in fall can sit through winter under a light cover and burst back into growth in early spring, weeks before a spring-sown crop is ready.
desc: Overwinter spinach for the earliest spring greens: sow cold-hardy spinach in early fall, protect young plants with row cover or straw, water before the ground freezes and uncover in spring for a harvest weeks ahead of spring-sown beds. Full list on the blog.

title: How to Freeze Fresh Herbs
subtitle: Garden Flavor All Winter
items: Freeze whole leaves on a tray
Or chop into ice cube trays
Top cubes with water or oil
Add frozen cubes to hot dishes
intro: Freezing keeps soft herbs like basil, parsley, chives and dill closer to fresh flavor than drying does. Frozen herbs go limp when thawed, so they are best stirred straight from the freezer into soups, sauces and stews. Keep herb-and-oil cubes frozen until you use them.
desc: How to freeze fresh herbs like basil, parsley, chives and dill: rinse and dry them, freeze whole leaves on a tray or chop them into ice cube trays topped with water or oil, then bag the cubes and drop them straight into winter soups and sauces. Full list on the blog.

title: Deep Litter Method for Coops
subtitle: A Warmer, Easier Winter Coop
items: Add a fresh layer when needed
Keep it dry: fix leaks fast
Clean it all out in spring
intro: With the deep litter method you keep adding clean bedding on top instead of cleaning the coop out every week. Stirred and kept dry, the layers slowly break down over winter, cut down on chores and give your hens a cushioned floor. If you ever smell ammonia, add bedding and improve ventilation.
desc: Deep litter method for backyard chicken coops: start with 4-6 inches of pine shavings, stir it every few days, add fresh bedding when it needs it, keep it dry with good high ventilation and clean it all out in spring for rich compost. Fewer winter chores for your hens. Full list on the blog.
